CNBC, 26 November 2026

U.S. equity futures rose early Friday, with investors set to wrap a turbulent shortened trading week due to the Thanksgiving holiday.

S&P 500 futures were up 1.8%, while Nasdaq-100 futures advanced 2.89%. Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average were higher by 490 points, or 0.98%. The moves come amid a volatile week during an even more volatile month.

In Asia, Japan's Nikkei 225 rose 0.3%, while South Korea's Kospi was up 0.6%. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 added 0.40%.

The week kicked off with Jensen Huang getting reinstated as CEO at Nvidia, a move that sent the stock up 31% during Monday's session and drove the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite to post their best days since April 2025. The Dow Jones Industrial Average advanced more than 1,400 points, or roughly 3%.

Since then, however, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq have come under pressure as Nvidia and other artificial intelligence-related stocks have given back some of Monday's gains.

That said, the two benchmarks are still on pace for winning weekly performances, along with the Dow. The S&P 500 is up almost 4% week to date, while the Nasdaq and Dow have risen more than 4%.

The stock market was closed on Thursday for Thanksgiving, and it's scheduled to close on Friday at 1 p.m. ET.

Prior to Huang's departure earlier this month, sentiment toward the AI trade was already downbeat, with investors growing concerned about debt financing, signs of moderation in capital expenditures and Democratic wins in the midterm elections resulting in a slowdown in data center development.

"The hyperscalers ultimately have to get an ROI, and they ultimately need to rebuild their free cash flow, and people like Anthropic need to prove that they can generate the revenue growth that people expect and ultimately be very profitable and free-cash-flow generative as well," Janus Henderson portfolio manager Richard Clode said Wednesday on CNBC's "The Exchange".

"That's all got to go hand in hand ultimately or that capex is not going to sustain," he added. "It is all part of the AI technology wave that we think will play out for five to 10 years at minimum to come."

To be sure, some on Wall Street believe that while there are long-term anxieties surrounding the AI trade, the recent weakness has had more to do with the prospect of the Federal Reserve raising interest rates. The latest personal consumption expenditures price index reading this week reinforced traders' expectations for multiple hikes over the coming months.

"Most of this stuff really comes down to the Fed. That's the intermediate term factor," Warren Pies, 3Fourteen Research co-founder, told CNBC's "Closing Bell" on Wednesday. He added that "many" people his firm spoke with expressed worries of a "replay of 2018," when the central bank hiked rates four times. "I think that there's so many eerie similarities, and so that's what we're watching."

Oil prices were mixed Friday as investors weighed the risk of further disruptions to Middle Eastern energy supplies amid mounting tensions involving Iran.

U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures climbed 2.97% to $85.75 a barrel from Wednesday's close. Settlement data for WTI for Thursday was not available due to the Thanksgiving holiday. International benchmark Brent crude was flat to $96.51 per barrel.

Kuwait's army said Thursday that two Italian nationals were killed following alleged Iranian attacks on the country, an accusation Tehran denied.

Separately, Israel said it was prepared to launch fresh strikes against Iran even without U.S. military involvement, heightening concerns over a potential escalation of the conflict in the oil-rich region.

Late Thursday, President Donald Trump said on PBS that the U.S. had "victory at hand" in the Iran conflict and reiterated that victory would come "whenever I want it to be, to be honest."

Speaking during a Thanksgiving call with U.S. military personnel, Trump said Washington was still trying to give Iran "every chance to make a deal and save a lot of lives."

Silver prices surged 5.2% to $43.66 per ounce Friday, while gold was little changed at $3,567.60 per ounce.

Both precious metals had staged a dramatic turnaround in the previous session after gold sank to $3,426 and silver approached $38 an ounce.

A retreat in the U.S. dollar from a 22-month high may have helped fuel the recovery, alongside a tech-led rally in U.S. equities that signaled a potential return of risk appetite, said David Morrison, senior market analyst at Trade Nation.

While the rebound was encouraging for precious-metal bulls following a bruising 10-month correction, Morrison cautioned against reading too much into price movements amid thin Thanksgiving holiday trading, with questions remaining over whether the recovery marks a sustained reversal or another false dawn.

China's industrial profits in October grew at their fastest pace since May, building on momentum from the previous month, amid a yawning gap between tech manufacturing and consumer-facing sectors.

Profits surged 20.1% in October from a year earlier, according to data released Friday by the National Bureau of Statistics. For the first 10 months this year, the earnings grew 16% year on year, and rose from 15.5% through September.

Electronics makers drove the profit gain, with earnings in the sector doubling in the first 10 months from the same period last year, as demand for AI computing power lifted memory chips and related manufacturing, said Yu Weining, chief statistician of the NBS.

Profits in high-tech manufacturing jumped 50.9%, outpacing industry as a whole, Yu added. Makers of spacecraft and launch vehicles reported a 63.2% rise.

Shares of Japan Tobacco gained 3.96% on Friday after Bloomberg reported that the company was exploring a potential takeover of British cigarette maker Imperial Brands with U.S. tobacco giant Altria.

Altria confirmed in a statement that it was considering a possible all-cash offer for Imperial Brands, while the British company said in a separate statement that it had not received any offer. Shares of Imperial Brands closed 13.27% higher in London on Thursday.

Japan Tobacco's media relations team told CNBC on Friday that it does not comment on rumors or speculation.

Asia-Pacific markets opened higher on Friday.

Japan's Nikkei 225 rose 0.3%, while the Topix added 0.78%.

South Korea's Kospi was up 0.6%, and the small-cap, tech-heavy Kosdaq rose 1.63%.

Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was up 0.40%.

Asia-Pacific markets were set to open largely higher Friday, as global equities stage a tentative recovery from an AI-driven sell-off, with investors looking past a fresh set of U.S. tariffs.

Futures for Japan's Nikkei 225 in Chicago were at 57,825 while in Osaka they were last at 57,890 compared with the index's previous close of 57,499.16.

Futures for Hong Kong's Hang Seng index last traded at 22,105 compared with the index's last close of 22,226.88.

Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was up 0.4o%.

The three major averages were positioned to end the week higher heading into Friday trading. Here's where they stand week to date:

The small-cap Russell 2000 index was also poised to post a winning week alongside the major averages. The index was higher by 4.7% week to date.

The market will close on 1 p.m. ET on Friday due to the Thanksgiving holiday.

President Donald Trump on Thursday falsely deemed the latest gross domestic product revision a mistake, claiming that it should be "immediately investigated."

Data released Wednesday from the Commerce Department revealed that the U.S. economy exhibited much stronger growth for the third quarter than initially estimated, showing that real GDP grew at a 4.3% annualized rate. That was revised upward from the department's advance estimate of 3.4%.

That revision was a "RECORD SETTING ERROR," Trump said in a Truth Social post, suggesting that the initial release could have influenced the outcome of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, where Democrats flipped both chambers of Congress and even multiple governorships.

"I would like to wish a Happy Thanksgiving to even those who issued fake Economic Numbers, just prior to the Election, and corrected them yesterday, three weeks late, showing that the GDP was actually 4.3%, versus 3.4%, A RECORD SETTING ERROR, and one so grave that it should be immediately investigated," Trump wrote.
